newsitem.title: USA: Ford unveils alternative vehicle program.
newsitem.headline: Ford unveils alternative vehicle program.

text.p: Ford Motor Co said Monday it hopes to perfect an alternative fuel vehicle by the middle of the next decade that would cost no more than a mid-size sedan.

Called the P2000 and costing between $150 million to $200 million to develop, the vehicle features an aluminum body and experimental aluminum-based engine. The P2000 gets its name from the fact that it weighs about 2000 pounds -- 40 percent less than a 1997 Taurus GL sedan.

At 113 cubic feet of interior passenger and luggage space, the vehicle will meet federal guidelines for a mid-sized car. It is expected to qualify as an ultra low emissions vehicle and get up to three times the fuel economy of the current family car.
Company officials stressed at a press conference at Ford's Scientific Research Laboratory the vehicle is designed to be something average car buyers could purchase.

"Our program is aimed at a high volume vehicle -- it is a Taurus-type vehicle," said Bob Mull, Ford's director of the Partnership for a New Generation of Vehicles, a joint venture between the federal government and the Big Three.
The biggest challenge remains high costs, Mull said. If the P2000 was on sale today, it would cost "many thousands of dollars" above the approximate $20,000 a Taurus GL costs now.
Funding for the P2000 have come from Ford and the federal government, Mull said, with Ford contributing more than half of that.

Ford is still experimenting with the vehicle's engine. The base powertrain combines an automated version of a five-speed manual tranmission with a new direct injection aluminum engine, or Diata configuration. Such an engine ignites with high heat instead of a spark plug.
Ford's Diata system, which runs on diesel fuel, is a four-cylinder, 1.2 liter engine that generates comparable performance to the 3.0 liter engine in the current Taurus.
To increase the vehicle's fuel efficiency, Ford plans to continue developing two different types of hybrid configurations that incorporate electric energy into the vehicle's propulsion system.
By this fall Ford plans to have 12 to 16 driveable prototypes. A more styled, aerodynamic version of the P2000 is due out by the end of 1998.

The P2000 is the most aggressive mass market alternative fuel program unveiled yet by one of Detroit's Big Three automakers. Chrysler Corp unveiled in January it is developing a gasoline-powered "fuel cell" program that could be commercially viable by 2010 or 2015.
General Motors Corp last September began selling the EV1 electric car, but has said it could be years before the car becomes practical for the mass market.
